questions.prompt: How does Ousterhout characterise complexity in software design?

options.text: Anything related to the structure of a system that makes it hard to understand and modify
The total number of lines of code in the system
The count of external libraries a system depends on
The time taken to compile the system

questions.explanation: Complexity is anything related to the structure of a software system that makes it hard to understand and modify it.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are listed as symptoms of complexity?

options.text: Change amplification
Cognitive load
Unknown unknowns
Faster compilation

questions.explanation: The three symptoms of complexity are change amplification, cognitive load, and unknown unknowns.

questions.prompt: According to the 'deep modules' principle, modules should have a simple interface and a comparatively more complex implementation.
questions.explanation: Modules should be deep: the interface (a cost) should be simple while the implementation (a benefit) is ideally much more complex.

questions.prompt: What is 'information leakage' in module design?

options.text: When a design decision is reflected in multiple modules, creating dependencies
When sensitive user data is exposed over the network
When comments reveal too much about the implementation
When a module logs its internal state

questions.explanation: Information leakage occurs when a design decision is reflected in multiple modules, which creates dependencies; the wider the interface the more info is leaked.

questions.prompt: Which mindset focuses on the long-term structure of the system rather than just making code work as soon as possible?

options.text: Strategic programming
Tactical programming
Move fast and break things
Temporal decomposition

questions.explanation: Strategic programming invests time in improving the design for the long-term structure; tactical programming focuses on working code as soon as possible.

questions.prompt: One strategy for handling errors is to 'define errors out of existence' by redefining a method's behaviour so no error is required.
questions.explanation: Defining errors out of existence means redefining behaviour so that no error condition arises, e.g. avoiding unnecessary exceptions like substring's IndexOutOfBoundsException.

questions.prompt: Which of these are dependency dimensions discussed in the lecture?

options.text: Structural (code-level) dependencies
Runtime / distribution dependencies
Data-level dependencies
Behavioral dependencies

questions.explanation: Four dependency dimensions are presented: structural, runtime/distribution, data-level, and behavioral.

questions.prompt: According to Gall's Law, a complex system that works...

options.text: Is invariably found to have evolved from a simple system that worked
Must always be designed completely from scratch
Cannot be maintained over time
Is always simpler than it appears

questions.explanation: Gall's Law: a complex system that works has invariably evolved from a simple system that worked; one designed from scratch never works.

questions.prompt: How is 'abstraction' defined in the lecture?

options.text: The selective removal of information — a simplified view that omits unimportant details
Adding as much detail as possible to an interface
Splitting one class into many small classes
Caching results to speed up a method

questions.explanation: Abstraction is the selective removal of information: omitting important info leads to unknowns, while keeping unimportant info leads to cognitive overload.

questions.prompt: 'Classitis' is the term for software that suffers from having too many (shallow) classes.
questions.explanation: Classitis is the disease of having too many classes; the Java I/O BufferedReader/InputStreamReader stack is the classic example.

questions.prompt: What is a 'pass-through method' red flag?

options.text: A method that does nothing but pass its arguments to another method
A method that catches and rethrows every exception
A method that is never called
A method with too many parameters

questions.explanation: A pass-through method does nothing but forward arguments to another method; it appears when the abstractions of adjacent layers are too close.

questions.prompt: The principle 'pull complexity downwards' holds that it is more important for a module to have a simple interface than a simple implementation.
questions.explanation: Pulling complexity downwards means a module should prefer a simple interface even at the cost of a more complex implementation.

questions.prompt: What should good comments primarily describe?

options.text: Things that are not obvious from the code itself
A line-by-line restatement of the code
The author's name and the date
The compiler flags used

questions.explanation: Comments should describe things not obvious in the code; they should not repeat the code, and higher-level comments enhance intuition.

questions.prompt: Which techniques are suggested for limiting the impact of exceptions?

options.text: Exception masking (handle low-level, e.g. retry)
Exception aggregation (one handler for different exceptions)
Just crash
Throw a new exception for every caller

questions.explanation: Limiting exceptions: masking, aggregation, just crash, and avoiding unnecessary exceptions — all reduce the places where exceptions must be handled.

questions.prompt: Which of these are structural (code-level) dependencies?

options.text: Implementation dependency (on a concrete class, not an abstraction)
Construction dependency (on how collaborators are created)
Compile-time dependency (must know another module at compile time)
Spatial dependency (on the location of another component)

questions.explanation: Structural dependencies are implementation, construction, and compile-time; spatial dependency is a runtime/distribution dependency.
